t.1.47.1: There, at their meeting with one another, having asked after each other's welfare, Sumati, at the end of their conversation, spoke these words to the great sage.
t.1.47.2: These two princes, may good fortune be with you, are heroes whose valor equals that of the gods, whose gait is like that of elephants and lions, and who resemble tigers and bulls.
t.1.47.3: With large eyes like lotus petals, bearing swords, quivers and bows, the two, who resembled the Aśvins in beauty, had reached the bloom of youth.
t.1.47.4: O sage, these two, who seem to have come to earth of their own will like two immortals from the world of the gods, how have they come here on foot, for what purpose, and whose sons are they?
t.1.47.5: Adorning this region as the moon and the sun adorn the sky, they resemble each other in stature, in gestures and in movements.
t.1.47.6: For what purpose have you two heroes, best among men, bearing excellent weapons, come upon this difficult path? I wish to hear it truly.
t.1.47.8: Hearing the words of Viśvāmitra, the king, filled with the highest joy, duly honored those two mighty sons of Daśaratha, who had arrived as supreme guests and were worthy of hospitable reverence.
t.1.47.7: Having heard those words of his, he related everything just as it had happened: the stay at Siddhāśrama and likewise the slaying of the Rākṣasas.
t.1.47.9: Then the two Rāghavas, having received the highest hospitality from Sumati, stayed there for one night and afterwards went on to Mithilā.
t.1.47.10: Seeing that beautiful city of Janaka, all the sages praised it, exclaiming, "Excellent, excellent!", and paid honour to Mithilā.
t.1.47.11: There, in a grove near Mithilā, Rāghava saw a hermitage, ancient, deserted and lovely, and he questioned the foremost of sages.
t.1.47.12: What is this place, resembling a splendid hermitage yet bereft of sages? I wish to hear, O blessed one, whose hermitage this was in former times.
t.1.47.13: Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, the great sage Viśvāmitra, of great splendor and skilled in speech, replied.
t.1.47.14: Come, I shall tell you; listen, Rāghava, to the truth of whose hermitage this is, which was cursed in anger by a great-souled one.
t.1.47.15: O best of men, long ago this was the hermitage of the great-souled Gautama, heavenly in appearance and greatly honored even by the gods.
t.1.47.16: And here, long ago, he practised austerities together with Ahalyā for many long years, O prince of great renown.
t.1.47.17: Knowing his absence, the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī, wearing the guise of the sage, spoke these words to Ahalyā.
t.1.47.19: O Raghunandana, recognizing the thousand-eyed one in the guise of a sage, the foolish woman consented, out of eagerness for the king of the gods.
t.1.47.18: Those who are filled with desire do not wait for the proper season, O well-composed one; I wish for union with you now, O slender-waisted one.
t.1.47.21: Then Indra, laughing, spoke these words to Ahalyā: "O lovely-hipped one, I am fully satisfied; I shall go back the way I came."
t.1.47.20: Then, with her heart fulfilled, she said to the best of the gods: "You have accomplished your purpose, O best of the gods; go quickly from here, O lord. O lord of the gods, you who bestow honor, always protect yourself and me."
t.1.47.22: Having thus united with her, O Rāma, he then went forth from the hut, hurrying in agitation, fearful on account of Gautama.
t.1.47.23: Then, as they were entering, he saw the great sage Gautama, unassailable even by gods and Dānavas, endowed with the power of austerity, drenched with the water of a sacred bathing-place, and blazing like a fire.
t.1.47.24: Seeing him, the lord of the gods became frightened, his face downcast with despair.
t.1.47.25: Then the sage, rich in good conduct, seeing the thousand-eyed Sahasrākṣa, ill-behaved and wearing the guise of a sage, spoke these words in anger.
t.1.47.26: O evil-minded one, since you have taken on my form and done this deed that should never be done, you shall become fruitless.
t.1.47.27: When the great-souled Gautama had spoken thus in anger, the testicles of the thousand-eyed one fell to the ground at that very instant.
t.1.47.28: Having thus cursed Śakra, he cursed his wife as well: "Here you shall dwell for many thousands of years."
